title: Thai Flood 2011: Rapid Assessment for Resilient Recovery and Reconstruction Planning
verified: 2026-11-02 via Crossref + World Bank OKR PDF
question: Damage, losses and recovery needs by sector after the 2011 floods, incl. finance and insurance
data: DALA sector assessments; interviews with BOT, Thai Bankers' Association, SFIs, OIC
identification: Descriptive damage and loss accounting; finance figures explicitly preliminary
main_finding: THB 1.43 trn (USD 46.5 bn) damage and losses, ~70% manufacturing, ~90% private; 2011 growth cut 1.1 pp (p.1). Expected NPL rise ~0.5% after BOT-allowed grace periods and restructuring (p.60). Under 1% of dwellings insured against natural disasters (p.59). Table 21 lists relief measures; SFIs front ~THB 183 bn (p.69)
how_my_project_differs: Aggregate and interview-based; no loan-level PD/LGD or satellite exposure; the project measures exposure of collateral and credit outcomes directly

authors: Chitchumnong, Piyayut; Hatairatana, Adisorn; Khangphukhieo, Wichit
title: Physical Climate Risk Stress Test: An Evidence-based Approach
question: Effect of the 2011 flood on a Thai bank's mortgage default; stress-test design
data: Proprietary Krungsri mortgage portfolio 2009-2013 (3-month default rate); river runoff at Nakhon Sawan for EVA
identification: Vintage (age-period-cohort) decomposition; predicted vs actual default; flood-affected vs non-affected; not quasi-experimental
main_finding: Small 2011Q4 default spike among relief-ineligible delinquents; post-flood default below predicted, attributed to debt relief (lower bound); affected borrowers riskier (upper bound). BOT soft loans THB 210 bn at 0.01%, on-lent at 3% (pp.7-8)
how_my_project_differs: Single bank, mortgages only, descriptive; no satellite collateral exposure, LGD, IFRS 9 staging or causal separation of flood and relief effects

title: Flood Risks and Impacts: Future Research Questions and Implication to Private Investment Decision-Making for Supply Chain Networks
venue: Background paper, Global Assessment Report on DRR 2013 (UNISDR)
question: How floods propagate through supply chains; Thailand 2011 automotive and electronics case
data: Industry, press and official data on inundated industrial parks and firms
identification: Descriptive case study plus methods review (IO, CGE, network)
main_finding: Seven industrial parks with 804 companies inundated (Table 3, p.8); as of 1 June 2012 some 17.5% of their factories could not resume operations (Table 4); firm impacts depended on preparedness and response
how_my_project_differs: Real-side propagation only; the project traces the shock into bank credit risk and capital. Spillovers threaten its control groups

authors: Noy, Ilan; Nguyen, Cuong; Patel, Pooja
title: Floods and Spillovers: Households after the 2011 Great Flood in Thailand
question: Direct and spillover effects of the 2011 flood on Thai households
data: Thai Household Socio-Economic Survey (repeated waves); 2012 self-reported exposure; satellite exposure indicators
identification: Comparison of directly flooded, spillover (community-flooded) and unaffected households
main_finding: Not stated in abstract (outcomes: income, expenditure, assets, debt, savings); no findings claimed
how_my_project_differs: Household welfare, not lender outcomes; the project uses a similar satellite exposure design for collateral and credit risk

title: What Does Debt Relief Do for Development? Evidence from India's Bailout for Rural Households
question: Does debt relief relax debt overhang and raise investment and productivity?
data: Household survey of beneficiaries of India's 2008 waiver (Rs 715 bn; ~45 m households)
identification: RD at 2-hectare pledged-land eligibility cutoff (100% vs 25% conditional relief)
main_finding: Debt falls persistently but investment and productivity do not rise; full-relief households borrow 6 pp less from formal sources and shift to informal credit; works through expectations about future access to credit
how_my_project_differs: Relief not tied to a disaster; the project studies relief interacting with physical damage to collateral

title: The Economic Effects of a Borrower Bailout: Evidence from an Emerging Market
question: Credit-market and real effects of India's 2008 farm-loan waiver
data: RBI district and bank-district credit data; regional productivity, wage and employment data
identification: District exposure from retrospective land-pledge eligibility rule; bank-district FE for local demand
main_finding: 1 s.d. more exposure: loans -4-6%, credit -13-16%; credit reallocated away from high-exposure districts; loan performance worsens among previously good borrowers; precise zero real effects; defaults track the electoral cycle
how_my_project_differs: Shows relief-induced moral hazard in an EM; the project asks whether flood relief similarly masks and defers PD/LGD effects and what that means for ECL

authors: Mukherjee, Saptarshi; Subramanian, Krishnamurthy; Tantri, Prasanna
title: Borrowers' Distress and Debt Relief: Evidence from a Natural Experiment
question: Effect of debt relief on later loan performance of distressed vs non-distressed borrowers
identification: RD on waiver cutoff dates; pre-waiver distress from exogenous borrower-level shocks
main_finding: Non-distressed beneficiaries' later loan performance worsens; distressed beneficiaries' improves
how_my_project_differs: Distress here is not flood-specific; satellite flood exposure could serve as the exogenous distress shock in Thailand

authors: Fiorin, Stefano; Hall, Joseph; Kanz, Martin
title: How Do Borrowers Respond to a Debt Moratorium? Experimental Evidence from Consumer Loans in India
venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 10358
verified: 2026-11-02 via Crossref + World Bank OKR PDF
question: Do moratoria create moral hazard; does it matter whether the lender or the regulator grants them?
data: Nationwide field experiment with Indian consumer lender (DMI Finance) during COVID moratorium
identification: RCT: lender-framed vs regulator-framed forbearance offers vs placebo/control; follow-up product experiment
main_finding: Lender-framed moratorium cuts default by 4 pp (7%); regulator-framed has no effect; later demand for lender's product 10 pp (27%) higher
how_my_project_differs: Consumer loans, no physical damage; the project studies mandated post-flood relief where collateral is also impaired

authors: Cherry, Susan; Jiang, Erica Xuewei; Matvos, Gregor; Piskorski, Tomasz; Seru, Amit
title: Government and Private Household Debt Relief during COVID-19
question: Scale, targeting and effects of household debt forbearance in the US during COVID-19
identification: Descriptive plus RD on CARES Act mortgage eligibility
main_finding: 70 m+ consumers (USD 2.3 trn of loans) entered forbearance; it helps explain low defaults relative to fundamentals; government subsidies raise forbearance by about a third; shadow banks gave less forbearance
how_my_project_differs: Advanced-economy pandemic shock with insurance and fiscal backstops; the project is an EM physical-hazard setting

authors: Chari, Anusha; Jain, Lakshita; Kulkarni, Nirupama
title: The Unholy Trinity: Regulatory Forbearance, Stressed Banks and Zombie Firms
question: Did RBI provisioning forbearance after the GFC let stressed banks hide bad loans?
identification: Variation in bank stress and industry share of failing firms
main_finding: Stressed banks used forbearance to conceal loans to insolvent firms; credit moved from healthy to the weakest firms
how_my_project_differs: Crisis rather than disaster forbearance; the project asks whether flood-related classification relief similarly delays stage migration and ECL

authors: Caballero, Ricardo J.; Hoshi, Takeo; Kashyap, Anil K.
title: Zombie Lending and Depressed Restructuring in Japan
question: Real effects of banks' evergreening of insolvent firms in Japan
identification: Industry zombie prevalence and firm-level regressions
main_finding: Zombie-dominated industries show depressed job creation and destruction and lower productivity; zombies depress non-zombies' investment and employment growth
how_my_project_differs: Standard reference for forbearance costs; not disaster-specific

authors: Hosono, Kaoru; Miyakawa, Daisuke; Uchino, Taisuke; Hazama, Makoto; Ono, Arito; Uchida, Hirofumi; et al.
title: Natural Disasters, Damage to Banks, and Firm Investment
question: Does a disaster-induced loan-supply shock reduce firm investment?
data: Japanese firm-bank data around the 1995 Kobe earthquake
identification: Firms outside the quake zone with main bank inside vs outside
main_finding: Firms outside the area whose main bank was inside invested significantly less
how_my_project_differs: Bank-damage channel in an advanced economy; the project studies borrower/collateral damage and relief in an EM

title: Extreme flood events once again drive high losses in 2021, yet 75% of flood risks remain uninsured
venue: Swiss Re news release on sigma 1/2022
question: Size of the flood protection gap
main_finding: Over the past decade 5% of severe flood losses insured in emerging markets vs 34% in advanced economies; Asia 7%; 2021 flood losses USD 82 bn economic vs ~USD 20 bn insured
how_my_project_differs: Motivates the thin-insurance setting; no credit outcomes

title: Emergency Decree on Financial Assistance to Persons Damaged by Floods B.E. 2555 (พระราชกำหนดการให้ความช่วยเหลือทางการเงินแก่ผู้ที่ได้รับความเสียหายจากอุทกภัย พ.ศ. 2555)
venue: Royal Gazette vol. 129 part 10 Kor pp.11-14 (26 Jan 2012)
verified: 2026-11-02 via BOT page + Royal Gazette PDF
question: Legal basis of BOT flood soft loans
main_finding: THB 300 bn cap; BOT lends to FIs at 0.01%; BOT share at most 70%; on-lending to flood-zone individuals and SMEs at most 3%; apply by 31 Dec 2013; repay within 5 years, by 31 Dec 2018 at the latest
how_my_project_differs: Defines a relief treatment with clear eligibility (flood-declared zones, lender participation) usable in identification

authors: นิธิสาร พงศ์ปิยะไพบูลย์ (romanisation not verified)
title: กองทุนประกันภัยพิบัติ: มาตรการฟื้นความเชื่อมั่น (The disaster insurance fund: a measure to restore confidence)
question: Design of the post-2011 disaster insurance fund
main_finding: Fund set up by decree of 26 Jan 2012 with THB 50 bn; cover capped at THB 100,000 for homes, 30% sub-limit for SMEs and industry; premiums 0.50/1.00/1.25%; sales from 28 Mar 2012; 2011 claims THB 480 bn
how_my_project_differs: Documents the post-2011 insurance backstop; take-up and effects on credit risk are unknown

title: ธปท. ผ่อนปรนหลักเกณฑ์และขอความร่วมมือให้สถาบันการเงินและ non-bank ให้ความช่วยเหลือลูกหนี้ที่ได้รับผลกระทบจากสาธารณภัย (BOT relaxes rules to help disaster-affected debtors)
question: Current BOT relief template for disaster-affected debtors
main_finding: Lower credit-card minimum payments, emergency personal-loan limits, restructuring or fee waivers for up to 12 months from the disaster-zone declaration; debtors may keep their pre-disaster classification
how_my_project_differs: Classification forbearance implies floods may not show up in staging; the project tests this with satellite exposure
